# A Day and a Week of AI-Era Engineering

Last verified: 2026-10-29 against the Claude Code CLI reference, best-practices and memory pages and Anthropic's building-effective-agents and context-engineering posts; `diffcap.sh` and `day.sh` re-run on macOS. The schedules and durations are the author's heuristics, labelled as such.

Starts from: nothing; I define each term where it first appears.
Builds on: engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 03 (the review checklist for AI-written diffs) and this module's lessons 01 to 05. The system of record (inbox, queue, statuses, task cards) is lesson 06; this lesson is the rhythm you run on top of it.

## The problem and why it matters

It is 10:40. You have four agent sessions open (an *agent* is a tool that reads your repository, edits files and runs commands from a plain-language request). Each one pings you: "done", "question", "tests failing", "done". You answer all four, merge two, and at noon you cannot say what you actually finished. Your own task, the one only you can do, got no hour at all.

That is the two failure modes at once. Too slow: you babysit. Too sloppy: you merge what you have not understood because the pings felt urgent. The fix is not a new tool. It is a schedule with rules about when you plan, when you build, when you review, and when you stop.

**Honest status of everything below:** the schedules, durations and ratios in this lesson are heuristics from my own experience and from common practice. They are not measured, not from a study, and yours will differ. The tool facts are from vendor docs I re-checked on 2026-10-29. Treat the times as a starting guess and change them after two weeks of your own notes.

## First principles

1. **Your attention is the scarce resource, not the agent's time.** Agents run in parallel; you read one diff at a time. Plan for review bandwidth (how much you can carefully read per day), not for how many agents you can start.
2. **Batch the interrupts.** Switching tasks costs time (my experience, not measured here). Agent pings wait for a scheduled review window instead of being answered on arrival.
3. **Every delegation has a budget and a stop condition.** Time, spend, diff size. Anthropic's "Building effective agents" says "it's also common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control".
4. **Write the handoff before you leave.** An agent session starts with no memory of yesterday, and so does tired-you. A note fixes both. Anthropic's context-engineering post describes the same idea for agents: notes "persisted to memory outside of the context window".
5. **Audit yourself, not the agent.** Sloppiness is a habit; five minutes of daily yes/no questions catches it before a reviewer does.
6. **Rhythm beats heroics.** A boring weekly loop (plan, checkpoint, review, clean up, learn) compounds.

## How it works

### The day in blocks (heuristic, adjust)

```
 time        block        rule
 08:45-09:00 plan         write the day plan
 09:00-11:00 deep work A  mine; agents run
 11:00-11:30 review       batch every ping
 11:30-12:30 deep work B  or meetings
 13:30-15:00 deep work C  hardest task
 15:00-15:30 review       batch; merge/reject
 15:30-17:00 flex         small stuff, mail
 17:00-17:20 handoff,     see the audit
             self-audit
```

Two deep-work blocks, two review batches, one flex block is the shape. The exact hours do not matter. What matters: a deep-work block has a start and an end, and nothing from an agent interrupts it.

### Morning: plan and set intent (15 minutes)

- Write one sentence: "By tonight, X is true that is not true now." If you cannot finish that sentence, you are not ready to delegate.
- Pick one to three tasks. Each gets a *check*: a command that exits 0 (success) only if the work is right. Lesson 02 shows how to write them.
- Decide which task is yours (needs judgment, or you want to learn it) and which is delegated.
- Read yesterday's handoff note first.

### Plan, delegate, review (the cycle)

```
 PLAN     you   small task + check
   |
 DELEGATE agent  works inside a budget
   |
 REVIEW   you   diff + run it yourself
   |
   +--> merge  or  reject + one-line why
```

Repeat the cycle per task. A task that ate its budget without passing the check is not "almost done". It is a spec problem: stop, rewrite the task smaller, and start again.

### Budgets and stop conditions

Decide these before you press enter, in the day plan:

```
 budget      example           how to enforce
 time        45 min wall       you check the clock
 spend       $5                tool flag or limit
 diff size   300 lines         script below
 attempts    2 failed fixes    your rule
```

Tool facts, as of 2026-10-29, from the Claude Code CLI reference: `claude -p "query"` queries via the SDK and then exits (non-interactive "print mode"); `--max-turns` is described as "Limit the number of agentic turns (print mode only). Exits with an error when the limit is reached."; `--max-budget-usd` is "Stop the run once estimated spend on API calls reaches this amount (print mode only)", checked against a client-side cost estimate "which can differ from your bill", and the page adds that spend can pass the cap, so leave headroom. Because both are marked print mode only, in an interactive session your stop rule is your own clock (check your plan or console for any account-level spend limit; I did not verify one). Other tools differ; the principle (a cap you set before starting) is what transfers.

The Claude Code best-practices page gives a one-line version of the attempts rule: "after two failed corrections run `/clear` and write a better prompt instead of a third." A third correction mostly adds a conversation full of failed attempts for the agent to re-read.

A diff-size cap is easy to script. This is `diffcap.sh` (plain sh):

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# diffcap.sh CAP [BASE]  exit 1 if changed lines (added+deleted) exceed CAP.
# BASE is a branch or commit (e.g. main). With no BASE it measures unstaged edits.
cap="${1:?usage: diffcap.sh CAP [BASE]}"; base="${2:-}"
n=$(git diff --numstat $base | awk '$1!="-"{s+=$1+$2} END{print s+0}')
echo "changed lines: $n (cap $cap)"
[ "$n" -le "$cap" ] || { echo "OVER BUDGET: stop, split the task"; exit 1; }
```

Run here on macOS in a throwaway git repo where I staged a 10-line file and then rewrote it to 200 lines (real output):

```text
$ sh ../diffcap.sh 500
changed lines: 190 (cap 500)        exit=0
$ sh ../diffcap.sh 100
changed lines: 190 (cap 100)
OVER BUDGET: stop, split the task   exit=1
```

Use it as `sh diffcap.sh 300 main` before you start reading a branch. Over the cap means send it back, not "read faster".

### Protect deep work from agent babysitting

- Start the agent, then close its window or move it to another desktop. Watching it is not review.
- Claude Code's best-practices page says "Watch the first minute, press `Esc` the moment Claude drifts". That is a good tradeoff: a minute of attention early, then leave.
- If an agent is blocked and waiting, it waits. A waiting agent costs nothing; your interrupted hour costs a lot (my experience).

### Batch your reviews

At each review window, in this order: (1) anything blocked on a question only you can answer, (2) diffs that passed their check, smallest first, (3) failed runs: read the log, rewrite the task, requeue. Use the checklist from engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 03 on every merge. The best-practices page (as of 2026-10-29) gives a reviewer prompt that checks a diff against a spec and ends "report gaps that affect correctness and skip style", and warns that a reviewer asked to find problems "will always find *something*".

### Handoff notes (midday and end of day)

The template is the `handoff` case in `day.sh` below: goal, done (with proof), in flight, next exact step, open question, do-not-do traps.

The "Next exact step" line is the valuable one: tomorrow you start by running a command, not by remembering. For work spanning several days the best-practices page says `/rename oauth-migration` in the session lets `claude --resume oauth-migration` from your shell pick it back up; for a fresh session, paste the note.

### The daily 5-minute self-audit

Five questions, yes or no, at the end of the day:

1. Did I run the code myself, not only the tests?
2. Can I explain every line I merged?
3. Did the new tests fail first (did I see red)?
4. Did I weaken, skip or delete a test, or let the agent do it?
5. Did I read the dependency and lockfile diff?

A "no" is not shame; it is tomorrow's first task (go back and do it) or a written reason. If you answer "no" to question 2 twice in a week, your batch is too big or your diffs are too large.

### The template file: `day.sh`

One plain-sh script writes today's plan, handoff or audit file into `notes/`, and refuses to overwrite.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# day.sh  usage: sh day.sh plan | handoff | audit
set -eu
kind="${1:-}"; d=$(date +%Y-%m-%d); mkdir -p notes
f="notes/$d-$kind.md"
[ -e "$f" ] && { echo "exists: $f (edit it, do not overwrite)"; exit 0; }
case "$kind" in
plan) cat > "$f" <<T
# Day plan $d
Intent (what is true tonight that is not true now?):

## Deep-work blocks (agents may run, I do not babysit)
- [ ] 09:00-11:00 :
- [ ] 13:30-15:00 :

## Delegations (each needs a stop condition)
| task | check it must pass | budget (min / \$ / diff lines) |
|---|---|---|
|  |  |  |

## Review batches (agent pings wait for these)
- [ ] 11:15  - [ ] 15:15  - [ ] 17:00

## Not today (parked, one line each)
T
;;
handoff) cat > "$f" <<T
# Handoff $d $(date +%H:%M)
Goal right now:
Done (with proof: command or link):
In flight (branch / worktree / session name):
Next exact step (the first command I will run):
Open question I must answer, not the agent:
Do NOT do (traps found today):
T
;;
audit) cat > "$f" <<T
# Self-audit $d  (5 minutes; answer yes / no / n-a)
1. I ran the code myself, not only the tests:
2. I can explain every line I merged:
3. New tests failed before the change (saw red):
4. I did not weaken, skip or delete a test:
5. I read the dependency and lockfile diff:
Any "no": fix it before closing, or write it in tomorrow's plan.
T
;;
*) echo "usage: sh day.sh plan|handoff|audit"; exit 2;;
esac
echo "wrote $f"
```

Run here on macOS (real output):

```text
$ sh day.sh plan
wrote notes/2026-10-29-plan.md
$ sh day.sh plan
exists: notes/2026-10-29-plan.md (edit it, do not overwrite)
$ sh day.sh audit
wrote notes/2026-10-29-audit.md
$ sh day.sh bogus
usage: sh day.sh plan|handoff|audit      exit=2
```

The generated files open as plain Markdown. I ran `plan`, `audit` and `handoff` and read the files back; I did not test it under shells other than macOS `sh`.

### One week

```
 Mon  PLAN      pick week's 3 outcomes,
                clear the inbox (06)
 Tue  build     day loop
 Wed  CHECKPOINT  30 min: on track?
                  cut or resize
 Thu  build     day loop
 Fri  REVIEW    merged vs reverted,
                clean instruction files,
                1 hour of learning
```

- **Monday plan (30 min).** From the queue (lesson 06), pick at most three outcomes for the week. Anything bigger is split.
- **Wednesday checkpoint (30 min).** For each outcome: done, on track, or off track? Off track means cut scope or resize now, not Friday. Also count how many reviews you skipped or rushed.
- **Friday review (45 min).** Look at what merged and what was reverted or reworked this week. For each rework, ask what the spec or check missed. Then clean your instruction files (the repo's `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`): delete anything a failure this week proved useless, add one line for each trap found. Anthropic's memory docs (as of 2026-10-29) say to "target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file" and that if two instructions contradict, "Claude may pick one arbitrarily". They also say Claude treats these files "as context, not enforced configuration" and point to a PreToolUse hook to block an action. A *hook* is a script the tool runs automatically at set points; *CI* is the automated checks your repository runs on every push. So a rule you cannot break needs a hook or CI check.
- **One hour of learning (Friday).** One primary source, one experiment (lesson 11 has the routine). Not social media.

### The weekly review template (copy it)

```markdown
# Week of 2026-11-02
Outcomes (3 max) and result: 1. ...  2. ...  3. ...
Merged this week: n.   Reverted or reworked: n. (why:)
Reviews I rushed or skipped: n. What made me rush?
Budget overruns (time / spend / diff): which task, why
Instruction-file edits (deleted / added): ...
Traps for next week:
One hour of learning: what, source, what I will try
```

## Worked failure scenario

Symptom: Thursday, a "small" change merged on Tuesday broke checkout for guest users. The revert took two hours.

1. **Detect:** the Friday review lists it under "reverted", and the Tuesday self-audit has two blanks (questions 1 and 3).
2. **Cause:** Tuesday had five agents running, three review windows collapsed into one at 17:00, and this diff was merged at 17:10 on "tests pass" alone. No red test first, never run by hand.
3. **Fix:** write the failing test for guest checkout, fix, run the flow by hand.
4. **Prevent:** cap parallel tasks at what one review window can hold (start with two or three; heuristic), add the diff-size gate, and make the self-audit a blocker for the Friday "done" count.

## Common mistakes (anti-patterns)

- **Slot-machine prompting.** Re-rolling the same vague prompt hoping for a good output. Stop after two failures; rewrite the spec.
- **Review fatigue.** Approving the fifth diff of the day with less care than the first. Cap review per window and put the riskiest diff first.
- **Context hoarding.** One endless session for everything. Use a fresh session per task (the best-practices page says `/clear` between unrelated tasks "costs nothing") and carry state in a note.
- **Parallelism beyond review bandwidth.** Ten agents, one reader. The unread diffs are a debt, not output.

## Try it (15 minutes)

1. Make a folder, save `day.sh` into it, run `sh day.sh plan` and fill it for tomorrow with one real task, a check, and three budgets.
2. Run `sh day.sh audit` and answer it for today, honestly.
3. Put the 5 questions at the top of your next PR description and answer them.
4. In two weeks compare your guessed times with what happened and change the schedule.

## Checklist

1. I write an intent sentence and a check before I delegate.
2. Every delegation has time, spend and diff-size limits.
3. Agent pings wait for a review batch.
4. I leave a handoff note with a "next exact step".
5. I run the 5-question audit daily and the weekly review on Friday.
